Introduction

Starting a Hospice Program in Tennessee represents a meaningful opportunity to serve individuals with terminal illnesses requiring end-of-life care and comfort while building a compliant, sustainable care business. Oversight and funding are administered by the Tennessee Health Facilities Commission (THFC), with reimbursement and program funding coordinated through the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), as hospice is a federally defined benefit.

With growing demand due to an aging population and Medicare reimbursement rates around $200-$220 per day for routine home care, Tennessee offers a market with growing demand and opportunities for specialized niches for providers prepared to navigate licensing, staffing, and compliance requirements. The state’s existing network of approximately 100 licensed providers indicates an established but not oversaturated market, with clear pathways for new entrants who can deliver high-quality, compassionate care.

This guide walks you through every step of launching a Hospice Program in Tennessee, from understanding complex regulations and licensing to building your interdisciplinary team, managing reimbursement, and preparing for state and federal inspections.

Table of Contents

  • Understand Tennessee’s Hospice Program Regulations
  • Choose the Type and Size of Your Program
  • Business Structure and Licensing
  • Develop a Comprehensive Business Plan
  • Secure a Suitable Facility or Office
  • Hire and Train Qualified Staff
  • Policies, Procedures, and Care Plans
  • Marketing and Referral Development
  • Maintain Compliance and Prepare for Reviews
  • Frequently Asked Questions

Section 1: Understand Tennessee’s Hospice Program Regulations

Tennessee regulates Hospice Programs through the Tennessee Health Facilities Commission (THFC), which is responsible for the initial licensure, renewal, and ongoing oversight of hospice agencies to ensure they meet state-specific operational standards. Because hospice care is primarily funded by Medicare, providers must also strictly comply with federal frameworks, most notably the CMS Hospice Conditions of Participation (CoPs) and HIPAA.

The regulatory framework emphasizes patient-centered care, comprehensive pain and symptom management, interdisciplinary team coordination, and meticulous compliance with the Medicare Conditions of Participation (CoPs). This includes detailed requirements for patient rights, the development and review of individualized plans of care, bereavement support for families, and robust quality assurance programs. Licenses in Tennessee typically require renewal every one to two years, contingent upon successful surveys and adherence to all regulations.

Section 2: Choose the Type and Size of Your Program

While “hospice” is a single license type in Tennessee, the services you provide are categorized into four distinct levels of care mandated by CMS. Each has different staffing, documentation, and reimbursement requirements. Understanding these is critical to your operational and financial model.

Tennessee supports multiple hospice service levels, including:

  • Routine Home Care (RHC): The most common level of care, provided in the patient’s residence (private home, nursing facility, or assisted living). Reimbursement is a daily per diem rate.
  • Continuous Home Care (CHC): Provided during periods of crisis to manage acute symptoms. This requires a minimum of 8 hours of direct nursing care in a 24-hour period and is reimbursed at a higher hourly rate.
  • General Inpatient Care (GIP): For pain or symptom management that cannot be handled in the home setting. This care is provided in a Medicare-certified hospital, skilled nursing facility, or dedicated inpatient hospice unit under contract with your agency.
  • Inpatient Respite Care: Short-term inpatient care provided to give the patient’s primary caregiver a break. This is limited to five consecutive days.

Program size is measured by Average Daily Census (ADC), which can range from a small startup census of 10-20 patients to a large, established agency serving 100+ patients. Demand is strongest in metropolitan areas like Nashville, Memphis, Knoxville, and Chattanooga due to high population density and large healthcare networks. Conversely, rural counties may offer significant entry opportunities with less competition, aligning with the identified market niche for rural hospice expansion.

Section 3: Business Structure and Licensing

Before you can serve patients, you must establish a formal business entity. Providers in Tennessee typically operate as a Limited Liability Company (LLC) or S-Corporation for liability protection and tax purposes. You must:

  • Register your business with the Tennessee Secretary of State.
  • Obtain an Employer Identification Number (EIN) from the IRS.
  • Secure required insurance coverage, including general liability, professional liability (malpractice), and workers’ compensation.
  • Submit a comprehensive licensing application to the Tennessee Health Facilities Commission (THFC). This includes detailed information about your business structure, key personnel, proposed services, and policies and procedures.

After state licensure, you must pursue Medicare certification to bill for services. This involves a rigorous survey conducted either by the state on behalf of CMS or by a CMS-approved accreditation organization like the Community Health Accreditation Partner (CHAP) or the Accreditation Commission for Health Care (ACHC). Licensing and certification timelines generally range from 6 to 12 months, depending on your readiness, the completeness of your application, and survey backlogs.

Section 4: Develop a Comprehensive Business Plan

A robust business plan is your roadmap to a successful launch and long-term sustainability. Startup costs for a new hospice agency in Tennessee typically range from $100,000 to $250,000. This covers accreditation fees, software, office rent, initial payroll, insurance, and legal/consulting fees. Note that this does not include the cost of building or purchasing an inpatient facility.

Operating expenses are driven primarily by your interdisciplinary team. Staffing represents approximately 60-70% of total costs, a critical factor in financial modeling. Your revenue will come from the per diem or hourly rates set by Medicare.

Typical reimbursement or revenue ranges in Tennessee include:

  • Routine Home Care: ~$200 – $220 per day
  • Continuous Home Care: ~$60+ per hour
  • Inpatient Respite Care: ~$470 per day
  • General Inpatient Care: ~$800 – $1,000+ per day

Providers who effectively manage their census and control costs while maintaining an average daily census that meets or exceeds 80% of projected capacity can generally achieve 12-20% gross margins. A realistic break-even point for a new hospice is typically between 12 and 18 months of operation.

Section 5: Secure a Suitable Facility or Office

Most new hospice agencies start by providing care in patients’ homes and do not operate their own inpatient facilities. Therefore, your primary physical location will be an administrative office. This office must meet specific requirements to ensure compliance and operational efficiency.

Facility requirements for a hospice administrative office include:

  • HIPAA-compliant record storage: A secure, locked area for paper charts and protected servers for electronic health records (EHRs).
  • Sufficient office space: Private offices for key administrative staff (Administrator, Director of Nursing) and a conference room for Interdisciplinary Group (IDG) meetings.
  • Accessibility: The office must be accessible to staff and compliant with ADA standards.
  • Proper Zoning: Ensure the location is zoned for commercial or business use.
  • Proximity: The location should be centrally located within your service area to minimize staff travel time.

If you plan to offer General Inpatient (GIP) or Respite care, you must secure contracts with one or more Medicare-certified facilities, such as a hospital or skilled nursing facility. These contracts must be in place before you can admit patients for these higher levels of care.

Section 6: Hire and Train Qualified Staff

Your Interdisciplinary Group (IDG) is the core of your hospice program. CMS regulations mandate specific roles to ensure holistic care for every patient and family. Your ability to recruit, train, and retain qualified professionals is paramount to your success.

Required roles for a hospice agency typically include:

  • Medical Director: A physician (MD or DO) who oversees the medical components of the hospice’s patient care program.
  • Administrator/Executive Director: Responsible for the day-to-day operations and overall management of the agency.
  • Director of Nursing/Clinical Director: A Registered Nurse (RN) who supervises all clinical staff and ensures quality of care.
  • Registered Nurse (RN) Case Managers: Manage a caseload of patients, developing and implementing the plan of care.
  • Social Worker (MSW): A Master’s-level social worker who addresses the psychosocial needs of the patient and family.
  • Spiritual Counselor/Chaplain: Provides spiritual support aligned with the patient’s and family’s beliefs.
  • Hospice Aides (CNAs): Provide personal care to the patient under the supervision of an RN.
  • Bereavement Coordinator: Manages the bereavement program, providing support to families for up to 13 months after the patient’s death.
  • Volunteer Coordinator & Volunteers: Manages the volunteer program, which is required by CMS to provide a minimum of 5% of all patient care hours.

Training requirements are extensive. All staff must receive orientation on the hospice philosophy, pain and symptom management, patient rights, infection control, emergency procedures, and their specific job duties. CMS also mandates ongoing continuing education to ensure staff remain current on best practices.

Section 7: Policies, Procedures, and Care Plans

Comprehensive, well-written policies and procedures are the foundation of a compliant hospice agency. These documents guide your team’s actions, ensure consistent care delivery, and are a primary focus during state and federal surveys. Tennessee and CMS require written policies covering all aspects of your operation.

Key policy requirements include:

  • Patient Admission, Transfer, and Discharge Criteria
  • Plan of Care Development and Review
  • Interdisciplinary Group (IDG) Meeting Procedures and Documentation
  • Medication Management and Reconciliation
  • Pain and Symptom Management Protocols
  • Patient and Family Rights and Grievance Procedures
  • Bereavement Services Program
  • Volunteer Program Management
  • Emergency Preparedness Plan
  • Quality Assurance and Performance Improvement (QAPI) Program

Individual care plans are central to hospice. They must be developed by the IDG in collaboration with the patient, family, and attending physician within 48 hours of admission. The plan must be documented, regularly reviewed (at least every 15 days), and updated to reflect the patient’s changing needs.

Section 8: Marketing and Referral Development

Hospice patients are not typically found through direct-to-consumer advertising. Instead, a successful hospice agency builds a strong network of professional referral sources. Your marketing efforts should be focused on business-to-business relationship building with key figures in the healthcare community.

Referrals for hospice care in Tennessee typically come from:

  • Hospitals: Discharge planners, case managers, and palliative care teams.
  • Skilled Nursing Facilities (SNFs): Directors of Nursing and social workers.
  • Assisted Living Communities: Executive Directors and wellness nurses.
  • Physician Offices: Especially oncologists, cardiologists, pulmonologists, and geriatricians.
  • Home Health Agencies: For patients who are no longer seeking curative treatment.

Successful providers build trust by focusing on impeccable compliance, clinical excellence, rapid response times, and clear communication. Demonstrating your ability to manage complex cases and support facility partners will generate a steady stream of referrals far more effectively than any public advertising campaign.

Section 9: Maintain Compliance and Prepare for Reviews

Oversight in the hospice industry is rigorous and continuous. Your agency will be subject to unannounced surveys from both state and federal bodies.

Oversight includes surveys conducted by the Tennessee Health Facilities Commission (THFC) for state licensure and a CMS-approved accreditation organization (like CHAP or ACHC) or the state survey agency for Medicare certification. Inspections are comprehensive and focus on tracing patient care from admission to discharge (or death) to ensure compliance at every step. Common deficiencies often relate to:

  • Incomplete or inconsistent documentation in the Plan of Care.
  • Failure to hold and document IDG meetings every 15 days.
  • Medication management errors or incomplete reconciliation.
  • Lack of evidence that all required disciplines (e.g., social work, spiritual care) were offered or provided.
  • Issues with volunteer program management and documentation of hours.

To succeed, you must foster a culture of continuous quality improvement and maintain audit-ready documentation at all times. Regularly conduct self-audits, review your QAPI data, and provide ongoing staff training to address any identified gaps before a surveyor finds them.

Section 10: Frequently Asked Questions

1. How long does it take to open a Hospice Program in Tennessee?

Typically, it takes 12-18 months from initial planning to becoming fully operational and achieving break-even. This includes 6-12 months for the intensive process of business formation, policy development, state licensure, and Medicare certification.

2. What licenses are required?

A Hospice license from the Tennessee Health Facilities Commission (THFC) is the primary state requirement. To receive payment for services, you must also achieve Medicare certification. This is done either through a direct survey by the state on behalf of CMS or by gaining accreditation from an approved body like CHAP or ACHC.

3. What reimbursement is available?

Reimbursement is primarily from Medicare and is paid on a per-diem or hourly basis depending on the level of care. In Tennessee, approximate rates are $200-$220/day for Routine Home Care, $60+/hour for Continuous Home Care, and higher per diem rates for General Inpatient and Respite Care.

Conclusion

Starting a Hospice Program in Tennessee is a complex but deeply rewarding venture. It requires careful planning, a thorough understanding of state and federal regulations, and unwavering operational discipline. The market shows clear signs of growing demand, offering a path to success for providers who prioritize compliance, invest in a highly-qualified interdisciplinary team, and build strong relationships within the local healthcare community. By focusing on compassionate, high-quality end-of-life care, you can build a business that not only thrives financially but also makes a profound difference in the lives of patients and their families.
